contribution: Cosmology as an application of quantum physics and nuclear physics: the redshift of galaxies $z = \tfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda_0}$ from the familiar spectral lines of hydrogen, the speed at small redshift $v = cz$, the Hubble–Lemaître law $v = H_0\,d$, which the student fits to the galaxies of the simulation, the estimate of the age $\tfrac{1}{H_0}$, the cosmic background radiation as a consequence of the formation of atoms, the nuclei of the Big Bang and the helium fraction from fusion, the elements of stars through the binding energy curve, and dark matter and dark energy as open questions.
learn: calculate the redshift, the recession speed and the distance of a galaxy with the Hubble–Lemaître law.
explain what the redshift of galaxies and the cosmic background radiation tell about the early universe.
explain at which stages hydrogen, helium and the heavier elements formed.
prior: An atom absorbs and emits only photons whose energy is the difference between two energy levels, so every element has its own spectral lines (chapter *Spectra reveal the energy levels of atoms*)
The fusion of light nuclei releases energy, because the binding energy per nucleon grows up to iron (chapter *Fission, fusion and nuclear power*)

activities.text: The spectrum of the light of a distant galaxy shows the familiar absorption lines of hydrogen, but they are in the wrong places. The red line, whose wavelength in the laboratory is $656.3\,\text{nm}$, appears at a wavelength of $669.4\,\text{nm}$, and the blue-green line has shifted from $486.1\,\text{nm}$ to $495.8\,\text{nm}$. The shifts are of different sizes, but each is $2.0\,\%$ of the wavelength of the line itself. The lines of almost every galaxy have shifted in the same way to longer wavelengths.
activities.question: What does the shift of the lines tell about the galaxies, and what can be concluded from it about the past of the universe?

activities.title: Recap: absorption lines
activities.prompt: When white light passes through hydrogen gas, dark lines are left in the spectrum at exactly certain wavelengths. Why exactly those?

choices.text: A hydrogen atom absorbs only photons whose energy is the difference between two of its energy levels.
choices.feedback: Correct. The energy levels are quantised, so the energies and wavelengths of the absorbed photons are characteristic of hydrogen (chapter *Spectra reveal the energy levels of atoms*). This is why the lines of hydrogen can be recognised in the light of a galaxy too, even when they have shifted.

choices.text: Hydrogen gas absorbs all wavelengths, but these a little more than others.
choices.feedback: The gas does not dim all wavelengths evenly. An atom absorbs only a photon whose energy corresponds exactly to the difference between two energy levels, so the other wavelengths pass through the gas (chapter *Spectra reveal the energy levels of atoms*).

choices.text: The electron of a hydrogen atom absorbs a photon whenever its energy is enough for ionisation.
choices.feedback: An ionising photon can have any energy, so it would not produce narrow lines. The lines come from transitions from one energy level to another: the energy of the photon must be exactly the difference between the levels (chapter *Spectra reveal the energy levels of atoms*).

choices.text: The colour of hydrogen gas determines which wavelengths are missing from the spectrum of the light.
choices.feedback: Thin hydrogen gas is almost colourless. The dark lines are due to the quantised energy levels of the atom: an atom absorbs only a photon whose energy is the difference between two levels (chapter *Spectra reveal the energy levels of atoms*).

activities.title: Prediction 1: redshift and distance
activities.prompt: The distances of the galaxies are known from other measurements. How do the redshift of a galaxy and the corresponding recession speed depend on the distance of the galaxy?

choices.text: They grow in direct proportion to the distance: twice as far away, twice as fast.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: galaxy 2 is $45\,\text{Mpc}$ away and recedes at $2840\,\text{km/s}$, galaxy 4 is $110\,\text{Mpc}$ away and recedes at $7560\,\text{km/s}$, and galaxy 8 is $275\,\text{Mpc}$ away and recedes at $19\,030\,\text{km/s}$. The points are close to a line through the origin.

choices.text: All galaxies have roughly the same redshift, because they recede equally fast.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the redshift of galaxy 1 is $0.0060$ and that of galaxy 8 is $0.0635$, more than ten times as much. A more distant galaxy recedes faster, because the expansion of space increases a large distance more than a small one.

choices.text: The nearest galaxies have the greatest redshift, and distant galaxies recede more slowly.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the nearest galaxy 1 recedes at $1800\,\text{km/s}$ and the most distant galaxy 8 at $19\,030\,\text{km/s}$. The speed grows with the distance; it does not decrease.

choices.text: Redshift and distance are not connected, because the galaxies move randomly.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the points clearly rise with the distance. Galaxies also have motion of their own, a few hundred kilometres per second, and it scatters the points a little around the line, but for distant galaxies the expansion dominates.

activities.title: Prediction 2: are we at the centre?

reveal.pending: The feedback opens when you have read the part *The universe is expanding* of the Theory summary.

activities.prompt: Almost all galaxies recede from us, and the faster the farther away they are. Which explanation fits the observation?

choices.text: The Milky Way is at the centre from which the Big Bang started, and the other galaxies are flying away from it.
choices.feedback: The observation does not require us to be at the centre. When space expands evenly, seen from any galaxy all the others recede at a speed proportional to the distance. The Big Bang was not an explosion at one point; space began to expand everywhere.

choices.text: Space is expanding everywhere, so seen from any galaxy the others recede in the same way.
choices.feedback: Correct. When all distances grow in the same proportion, a galaxy that is twice as far away moves twice as far in the same time, whichever galaxy the observer is in. The expansion has no centre.

choices.text: The gravity of the Milky Way repels the other galaxies, and the repulsion is greater the farther away they are.
choices.feedback: Gravity pulls objects towards each other and does not repel them, and it weakens as the distance grows. Galaxies recede because space itself expands; gravity, on the contrary, holds galaxies and galaxy clusters together.

activities.text: Choose a galaxy. Compare its hydrogen lines with the laboratory lines, and collect in the graph the speeds of the galaxies as a function of distance. Finally fit a line through the origin to the points.
activities.howto: Choose a galaxy $1$–$8$ from the *Galaxy* menu. On the map the galaxy is circled, and a light wave travels from it to the Milky Way, its wavelength stretching on the way. In the spectrum picture, the absorption lines of hydrogen in the laboratory are above and the same lines in the light of the galaxy below; the dashed line shows the shift of the red $\text{H}\alpha$ line. The readout shows the distance of the galaxy $d$, the wavelength and shift $\Delta\lambda$ of the $\text{H}\alpha$ line, the redshift $z$ and the speed $v$. Every galaxy you choose leaves a point $(d, v)$ in the graph. The slider *Slope of the line $H_0$* turns the line $v = H_0\,d$ through the origin: adjust it to pass through the middle of the points. *Speed* changes only the motion of the light wave, and *Clear the graph* removes the points.
activities.model: The galaxies and their distances are invented, but their speeds follow the Hubble–Lemaître law, to which a motion of its own of a few hundred kilometres per second has been added for each galaxy. The distances are assumed to be known accurately, as if they had been measured, for example, from the brightness of supernovae. The redshifts are small, under $0.1$, so the speed is $v = cz$. The map shows the directions and distances of the galaxies in roughly the right proportion, and the stretching of the light wave is exaggerated eightfold. The readings are values of the model and not measurements.
activities.calc: Every hydrogen line appears at the wavelength $\lambda = \lambda_0\,(1 + z)$, so the redshift is $z = \tfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda_0}$ and the speed $v = cz$, where $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{5}\,\text{km/s}$. The laboratory wavelengths are $\text{H}\alpha$ $656.3\,\text{nm}$, $\text{H}\beta$ $486.1\,\text{nm}$, $\text{H}\gamma$ $434.0\,\text{nm}$ and $\text{H}\delta$ $410.2\,\text{nm}$. From the slope of the line, the time $\tfrac{1}{H_0}$ is calculated by substituting $1\,\text{Mpc} = 3.086 \cdot 10^{19}\,\text{km}$ and $1\,\text{a} = 3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{s}$; it is shown in billions of years.

activities.title: Experiment: redshift and distance
activities.intro: Test prediction 1. Choose the galaxies one at a time and record for each the distance $d$, the shift of the $\text{H}\alpha$ line $\Delta\lambda$, the redshift $z$ and the speed $v$, for at least five galaxies, preferably all eight. See how the points settle in the graph.

question.prompt: Adjust the slider $H_0$ until the line passes through the middle of the points, so that about as many points are left on each side of the line. What is the Hubble constant given by your fit, in the unit $\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$?
hints: The line must pass through the origin, because our own galaxy ($d = 0$) has no recession speed.
Do not try to hit a single point: the most distant galaxies determine the slope most accurately, because their own motion is small compared with the speed of the expansion.
Check your fit by calculating the ratio of the speed to the distance of the most distant galaxy: $19\,030\,\text{km/s} : 275\,\text{Mpc}$.

mistakes.feedback: This is the initial value of the slider. The line stays clearly below the points: adjust the slope to be greater until there are points on both sides of the line.
You calculated the ratio of the distance to the speed. The Hubble constant is the speed divided by the distance, $H_0 = \tfrac{v}{d}$.

question.solution:
**Given:** the values of the model for the eight galaxies of the simulation, for example galaxy 4: $d = 110\,\text{Mpc}$, $v = 7560\,\text{km/s}$ and galaxy 8: $d = 275\,\text{Mpc}$, $v = 19\,030\,\text{km/s}$

**Asked:** the Hubble constant $H_0$, that is, the slope of the fitted line in the unit $\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$

**Principle:** The graph of the Hubble–Lemaître law $v = H_0\,d$ is a line through the origin, because at distance zero there is no recession speed. In real data sets the measured points do not usually lie exactly on the same line; here the scatter comes from the own motion of the galaxies. This is why the slope is read from the fitted line and not from two adjacent points.

**Reading the graph:** When $H_0$ is about $70\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$, the line passes through the middle of the points: galaxies 1, 3, 5 and 7 are slightly above the line and galaxies 2, 4, 6 and 8 slightly below. From the line we read the point at distance $d = 200\,\text{Mpc}$, where $v = 14\,000\,\text{km/s}$.

**Formula:** $v = H_0\,d$, so $H_0 = \dfrac{v}{d}$

**Conversions:** None needed: the speed is in kilometres per second and the distance in megaparsecs, as in the unit asked.

**Substitution:** $H_0 = \dfrac{14\,000\,\text{km/s}}{200\,\text{Mpc}} = 70\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$

**Answer:** about $70\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$; a fit by eye gives two significant figures, and a difference of a few units is acceptable.

**Reasonableness:** For the most distant galaxy $19\,030 : 275 \approx 69$ and for galaxy 4 $7560 : 110 \approx 69$, close to the fit. The least-squares line through the origin gives $69.8\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$. In the readout $\tfrac{1}{H_0} \approx 14 \cdot 10^{9}\,\text{a}$, close to the age of the universe, $13.8$ billion years.

activities.title: Conclusion: the Hubble–Lemaître law
activities.prompt: Write, based on your table and the graph: How does the speed of a galaxy depend on its distance? Why are the points not exactly on a line? What does the slope $H_0$ of your fitted line tell about the universe?
activities.model: In the values of the model the speed grows in direct proportion to the distance: galaxy 2 ($45\,\text{Mpc}$) recedes at $2840\,\text{km/s}$, galaxy 4 ($110\,\text{Mpc}$) at $7560\,\text{km/s}$ and galaxy 8 ($275\,\text{Mpc}$) at $19\,030\,\text{km/s}$. The points are close to the line $v = H_0\,d$ through the origin, whose slope is about $70\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$. The points deviate from the line by a few hundred kilometres per second, because the galaxies also have motion of their own; for distant galaxies it is small compared with the speed of the expansion. Proportionality means that all distances grow in the same proportion, that is, space is expanding. Extension note: if the speed of the expansion had stayed the same, all the galaxies would have been in the same place a time $\tfrac{1}{H_0} \approx 14$ billion years ago.
criteria: I show with the values of the model that the speed is directly proportional to the distance and the points are close to a line through the origin.
I explain the scatter of the points by the own motion of the galaxies.
I give the slope of my fit with its unit.
I call the numbers of the simulation values of the model and not my own measurements.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the values of the model in the experiment and with the theory. Then return to the question at the beginning: what does the redshift of galaxies tell about the past of the universe, and why does it not mean that we are at the centre?

activities.title: Extension: find the error
activities.prompt:
A student estimates the age of the universe when $H_0 = 70\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$. She substitutes $1\,\text{Mpc} = 3.086 \cdot 10^{22}\,\text{m}$ and writes

$$\begin{aligned} &t = \frac{1}{H_0} = \frac{3.086 \cdot 10^{22}}{70}\,\text{s} \\ &= 4.4 \cdot 10^{20}\,\text{s} \\ &\approx 1.4 \cdot 10^{13}\,\text{a} \end{aligned}$$

The result is a thousand times too large. Where is the error?

choices.text: The megaparsec has been changed into metres, but the speed is still in kilometres per second.
choices.feedback: Correct. The units must cancel: when $1\,\text{Mpc} = 3.086 \cdot 10^{19}\,\text{km}$ is divided by the speed $70\,\text{km/s}$, the result is $4.4 \cdot 10^{17}\,\text{s} \approx 1.4 \cdot 10^{10}\,\text{a}$. When the units are written out in the substitution, the error is revealed: $\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{km/s}}$ is not a second.

choices.text: The estimate of the age is $\tfrac{1}{2H_0}$ and not $\tfrac{1}{H_0}$, so the result must be halved.
choices.feedback: The estimate $t = \tfrac{d}{v} = \tfrac{1}{H_0}$ assumes a constant speed, and that is the intention here. Halving would not correct an error of a factor of a thousand. The error is in the units: the megaparsec is in metres but the speed in kilometres per second.

choices.text: The seconds have been changed into years wrongly, because a year has $3.156 \cdot 10^{4}\,\text{s}$.
choices.feedback: A year has $365 \cdot 24 \cdot 3600\,\text{s} \approx 3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{s}$, so the conversion into years is correct. The error comes before it: the megaparsec has been changed into metres, although the speed is in kilometres per second.

choices.text: The Hubble constant should first have been multiplied by the speed of light $c$.
choices.feedback: The speed of light is needed when the speed is calculated from the redshift, $v = cz$, but not in the estimate of the age, $t = \tfrac{1}{H_0}$. The error is in the units: the megaparsec is in metres but the speed in kilometres per second.

activities.title: Transfer: the calcium line
activities.prompt: In the spectra of galaxies, lines of other elements can be seen in addition to hydrogen. The wavelength of the violet K line of the calcium ion in the laboratory is $393.4\,\text{nm}$. In the light of the galaxies of a galaxy cluster, the line appears at a wavelength of $401.3\,\text{nm}$. How far away is the galaxy cluster, when $H_0 = 70\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$ and $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{5}\,\text{km/s}$? Give the answer in megaparsecs.
hints: Which quantity tells how much the line has shifted relative to its own wavelength? You need the laboratory wavelength for it.
From the redshift you get the speed $v = cz$, and from the Hubble–Lemaître law $v = H_0\,d$ the distance.

mistakes.feedback: You divided the shift by the wavelength $401.3\,\text{nm}$ measured from the light of the galaxy. The redshift is calculated relative to the laboratory wavelength: $z = \tfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda_0}$, where $\lambda_0 = 393.4\,\text{nm}$.

You used the speed of light in metres per second. Because the Hubble constant is in the unit $\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$, the speed must be in kilometres per second: $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{5}\,\text{km/s}$.
This is the recession speed of the galaxy cluster in kilometres per second. The distance is obtained by dividing it by the Hubble constant: $d = \tfrac{v}{H_0}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** the K line of calcium in the laboratory $\lambda_0 = 393.4\,\text{nm}$ and in the light of the galaxy cluster $\lambda = 401.3\,\text{nm}$, $H_0 = 70\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{5}\,\text{km/s}$

**Asked:** the distance $d$ of the galaxy cluster in megaparsecs

**Principle:** The redshift is the same for every line of an element, so from the line of calcium too we get $z = \tfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda_0}$. The redshift is small, so the speed is $v = cz$, and according to the Hubble–Lemaître law the distance is the speed divided by the Hubble constant.

**Formula:** $z = \dfrac{\lambda - \lambda_0}{\lambda_0}$, $v = cz$ and $v = H_0\,d$, so $d = \dfrac{c\,(\lambda - \lambda_0)}{H_0\,\lambda_0}$

**Conversions:** None needed: the nanometres cancel in the redshift, and when the speed of light is in kilometres per second, the kilometres per second cancel and the distance comes out in megaparsecs.

**Substitution:** $z = \dfrac{401.3\,\text{nm} - 393.4\,\text{nm}}{393.4\,\text{nm}} = \dfrac{7.9\,\text{nm}}{393.4\,\text{nm}} = 0.020081$, $v = 2.998 \cdot 10^{5}\,\text{km/s} \cdot 0.020081 = 6020\,\text{km/s}$ and $d = \dfrac{6020\,\text{km/s}}{70\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}} = 86.0\,\text{Mpc}$

**Answer:** $86\,\text{Mpc}$, two significant figures, as in the shift $7.9\,\text{nm}$ and in the Hubble constant $70\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$.

**Reasonableness:** The shift is about $2\,\%$ of the wavelength, so the speed is about $2\,\%$ of the speed of light, that is, $6000\,\text{km/s}$, and $6000 : 70 \approx 86$. The distance is of the same order of magnitude as the nearest large galaxy clusters, about $100\,\text{Mpc}$.

activities.text: Practise on three levels. Level 1 tasks use one equation, level 2 tasks combine two equations or convert units, and level 3 requires reasoning.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: The cosmic background radiation was released about $380\,000$ years after the Big Bang, when the temperature of the gas was about $3000\,\text{K}$. Why is it now observed as microwaves and not as visible or infrared light?

choices.text: The expansion of the universe has stretched its wavelengths by a factor of about $1100$.
choices.feedback: Correct. The radiation was released as near-infrared and red light, but the expansion of space has stretched every wavelength on the way. Now the radiation corresponds to a body at a temperature of $2.725\,\text{K}$.

choices.text: The radiation loses energy as it collides on the way with gas clouds between the galaxies.
choices.feedback: When atoms formed, very few free electrons were left for the photons to scatter from. So the radiation has travelled almost without collisions since then. The wavelengths have grown because space expands and stretches them.

choices.text: The radiation is now emitted by cold dust that has cooled close to absolute zero.
choices.feedback: The background radiation is not produced now; it was released already $380\,000$ years after the Big Bang. Cold dust would also not radiate in almost exactly the same way from every direction. The microwaves are the original radiation, stretched by the expansion.

choices.text: The stars of the Milky Way emit microwaves that drown out the original light.
choices.feedback: The radiation of the Milky Way is concentrated in the direction of the plane of the galaxy, but the background radiation arrives almost evenly from every direction. It is radiation released after the Big Bang, whose wavelengths the expansion has stretched.

activities.title: 2. Read the Hubble constant from a graph
activities.prompt: The graph shows the recession speed $v$ of nine galaxies as a function of the distance $d$, and a line through the origin has been fitted to the points. What is the Hubble constant according to the graph, in the unit $\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$?
hints: The Hubble constant is the slope of the line, $H_0 = \tfrac{v}{d}$.
Read the slope from a point of the fitted line, not from a single galaxy. Choose a point on the line that is at an intersection of the grid lines.
The line passes through the point $d = 250\,\text{Mpc}$, $v = 18\,000\,\text{km/s}$.

mistakes.feedback: You divided the distance by the speed. The slope is the quantity of the vertical axis divided by the quantity of the horizontal axis: $H_0 = \tfrac{v}{d}$.

activities.practice: Practise with level 1 tasks that use the Hubble–Lemaître law.
activities.solution:
**Given:** a graph of the speed $v$ of galaxies as a function of the distance $d$ and a line through the origin fitted to the points

**Asked:** the Hubble constant $H_0$ in the unit $\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$

**Principle:** According to the Hubble–Lemaître law $v = H_0\,d$, the Hubble constant is the slope of the line through the origin in the $(d, v)$ graph. The own motion of the galaxies scatters the points, so the slope is read from the fitted line and not from a single point.

**Reading the graph:** The line passes through the origin and the grid point $d = 250\,\text{Mpc}$, $v = 18\,000\,\text{km/s}$. At the origin $v = 0$, so the slope is the ratio of these readings.

**Formula:** $v = H_0\,d$, so $H_0 = \dfrac{v}{d}$

**Conversions:** None needed: the speed is in kilometres per second and the distance in megaparsecs, as in the unit asked.

**Substitution:** $H_0 = \dfrac{18\,000\,\text{km/s}}{250\,\text{Mpc}} = 72\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$

**Answer:** $72\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$, two significant figures, which can be read from the graph.

**Reasonableness:** Another point of the line, $d = 125\,\text{Mpc}$ and $v = 9000\,\text{km/s}$, gives the same slope. The value is close to the known value of $70\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$, and the corresponding estimate of the age $\tfrac{1}{H_0}$ is about $13.6$ billion years.

activities.title: 3. Explain: where does gold come from?
activities.prompt: The gold-197 nuclei in a gold ring contain $197$ nucleons. Why was gold not formed in the Big Bang or in the fusion of a star like the Sun? Where was it formed? Use the binding energy curve in your reasoning.
activities.model: After the Big Bang, fusion lasted only about $20$ minutes, and mostly helium was formed in it. In stars, fusion releases energy only as long as the nucleus that forms is more tightly bound than the starting nuclei, that is, as long as the binding energy per nucleon grows. The peak of the binding energy curve is at iron-56, about $8.8\,\text{MeV}$, so forming nuclei heavier than iron by fusion would require energy and not release it. In addition, a star like the Sun fuses only hydrogen into helium and finally helium into carbon and oxygen. Gold formed in neutron capture: when a nucleus quickly captures many neutrons and some of them change into protons in beta minus decay, heavy nuclei are formed. Such rapid neutron capture takes place in supernovae and in neutron star collisions. The gold of the ring was therefore formed in stellar explosions or collisions before the formation of the Solar System.
criteria: I explain with the binding energy curve that fusion releases energy only up to iron.
I state that the fusion of the Big Bang lasted only minutes and produced mostly helium.
I name neutron capture, and supernovae or neutron star collisions, as the birthplaces of gold.

activities.text: Finally, two quick questions. Answer first yourself and only then open the answer.
